title: NHAI Guidelines to Standardise Design and Infrastructure for Multi-Lane Free Flow Tolling on Four-Lane and Above National Highways
subtitle: Standardised infrastructure and design to facilitate seamless, technology led, barrier-free toll collection system across upcoming and ongoing National Highway projects
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 NOV 2026 5:13PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Paving way for wider adoption of barrier-less Multi-Lane Free Flow (MLFF) tolling system across the country, National Highways Authrity of India (NHAI) has issued guidelines to standardise design and infrastructure of toll plazas on four-lane and above National Highways. The guidelines will ensure that upcoming and ongoing National Highway projects are equipped to support MLFF based barrier-free toll collection without requiring vehicles to stop at toll booths. The initiative is aimed at eliminating traffic queues and waiting time, reducing fuel consumption at toll plazas, while making National Highway journeys safer and more seamless.
The guidelines prescribe uniform requirements for toll plaza layouts, lane configuration, gantries, road infrastructure, lighting, signage and supporting facilities. It also lays down an implementation framework for upcoming and ongoing National Highway projects.
Standardized design for different National Highway configurations
The policy circular lays down standardised guidelines for the layout and infrastructure of Barrier-Less Toll Plazas across different configurations of National Highways. These guidelines broadly prescribe the plaza layout, number of tolling lanes, provision and placement of gantries, and associated road safety features, signage and lighting arrangements to ensure uniformity in the design and facilitate seamless implementation of barrier-less tolling across the country.
With vehicles being tolled without the need to stop at physical barriers, the number of lanes required at a toll plaza has been rationalised in comparison to conventional toll plazas, facilitating more efficient utilisation of available space and improving traffic movement through the tolling zone.
Implementation on National Highway projects
The guidelines will apply to all future and under construction projects. Projects at the Detailed Project Report (DPR) stage will incorporate the new design in their documents, while projects already awarded or under construction will adopt the changes through applicable contractual provisions. NHAI field offices have been directed to incorporate the prescribed requirements in upcoming projects and facilitate their adoption in ongoing projects.
Emphasis on safety and user convenience
The policy circular emphasize the provision of adequate lighting, advance information and guidance to highway users through appropriate signage and Electronic Variable Message Signs (VMS) at toll plazas. These measures are aimed at enhancing visibility, keeping road users informed about the tolling zone and ensuring safe and smooth movement of vehicles. The guidelines also provide for construction of an administrative building-cum-operations and maintenance centre operational and maintenance infrastructure for efficient management of toll plaza operations.
Earlier, NHAI released comprehensive guidelines for planning and designing of High-Speed Access controlled National Highways, other than Expressways. The guidelines aimed to bring uniformity in standards for preparation of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) of upcoming high-speed National Highway corridors to bring greater consistency in technical standards and strengthen road safety.
The introduction of standardized infrastructure and design framework for MLFF toll plazas mark an important step towards creating a uniform framework for barrier-less tolling, providing seamless travel experience to National Highway users and enhancing overall efficiency of toll operations across the country.

title: Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat
subtitle: Two Years of Collective Action Towards a Child-Marriage-Free India
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 NOV 2026 5:33PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Child marriage remains a persistent social challenge in India, affecting girls' health, education and future opportunities. However, its prevalence among women aged 20-24 years who got married before the age of 18 has declined from 23.3 per cent in NFHS-5 (2019-21) to 20.1 per cent in NFHS-6 (2023-24). Launched on 27 November 2024, the Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat campaign contributes to strengthening efforts to prevent child marriage through legal safeguards, public awareness and community participation. 6.85 lakh awareness programmes were conducted, 12.47 crore participants were reached and 42.01 lakh pledges were registered. As it completes two years, the campaign continues to advance the national goal of a child-marriage-free India by 2030.
Towards a Child-Marriage-Free India
Child marriage remains a persistent social challenge in India, even though it is prohibited by law. As per the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6), 2023-24, 20.1 per cent of women aged 20-24 years were married before the age of 18, down from 23.3 per cent in NFHS-5 (2019-21), a fall of
3.2 percentage points
.
The practice exposes girls to serious health risks, particularly from early pregnancy, increases vulnerability to domestic violence, interrupts education, and perpetuates cycles of poverty and gender inequality.
India’s response has therefore been layered: a law that prohibits and punishes, a scheme that changes how girls are valued, and, since November 2024, Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat (BVMB), a national campaign that brings the two together in community action.
The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 (PCMA)
The legal answer to this challenge is the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, the statutory foundation for action against child marriage. It replaced the Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929 (Sarda Act), shifting the legal approach from merely restraining child marriage to prohibiting it, while offering stronger protection and relief to victims.
Who is a “child”:
A male who has not completed 21 years of age and a female who has not completed 18 years of age. A child marriage is one in which either contracting party is a child.
Status of the marriage:
A child marriage is voidable at the option of the party who was a child, who may petition the District Court, generally within two years of attaining majority. It is void in specified circumstances, such as where the child has been trafficked, taken by force or deceit, or used for immoral purposes.
Offences and penalties:
Offences under the Act are cognizable and non-bailable. An adult male marrying a child, and persons who solemnise, perform, abet, promote or attend a child marriage (including parents and guardians), are liable to rigorous imprisonment of up to two years and/or a fine of up to ₹1 lakh. Women offenders are not liable to imprisonment.
Relief for victims:
The Act provides for maintenance, residence and custody arrangements, and the children of such marriages remain legitimate.
Prevention through injunctions:
Judicial Magistrates are empowered to issue injunctions to stop an impending child marriage. District Magistrates and Child Marriage Prohibition Officers play an important role in prevention, particularly during mass marriage occasions and festivals such as Akshaya Tritiya. They do so through timely intervention, awareness and coordination with local authorities.
Child Marriage Prohibition Officers (CMPOs):
Section 16 of the Act empowers State Governments to appoint CMPOs by notification in the Official Gazette. Their statutory duties include preventing the solemnisation of child marriages, collecting evidence for prosecution, counselling individuals and communities, creating awareness, sensitising communities, and furnishing periodic returns and statistics. Effective implementation therefore demands not only enforcement after a violation, but also preventive outreach, community vigilance and prompt intervention before a marriage takes place.
Supreme Court Framework:
In its judgment dated 18 October 2024 in Society for Enlightenment and Voluntary Action & Another v. Union of India & Others (W.P. (C) No. 1234 of 2017), the Hon'ble Supreme Court issued a comprehensive framework for States and Union Territories. It emphasised dedicated, full-time CMPOs at district and sub-district levels. It also emphasised special units for coordination, monitoring and grievance redressal, multi-sectoral awareness campaigns, and training of key functionaries. Technology-enabled reporting and databases of areas at risk were also emphasised.
The judgment shifts the focus decisively from punishment towards prevention, protection and empowerment. Yet law alone cannot change the social norms that sustain the practice, which is where the education and empowerment of girls come in.
Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (BBBP)
While law prohibits child marriage, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (BBBP) works to change the social attitudes that sustain it. BBBP was launched on 22 January 2015, to address the Child Sex Ratio and the wider empowerment of girls and women across the life cycle.
BBBP is a multi-sectoral initiative led by the Ministry of Women and Child Development as the nodal ministry. It works in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Ministry of Education, Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, and Ministry of Minority Affairs. The scheme is implemented as a component of Mission Shakti. It focuses on awareness generation, advocacy, community mobilisation and behavioural change. It also promotes the survival, protection and education of the girl child.
Prevention of child marriage is closely linked to these objectives. Promoting girls’ education, addressing school dropouts, challenging discriminatory social norms and encouraging families to value the girl child all help to delay marriage and widen opportunities for adolescent girls.
BVMB builds on this foundation by adding a sharper operational focus on child marriage and a coordinated statutory and community-level response. It is this coming together of the law, the scheme and community action that gave rise to the national campaign.
A Collective Commitment to End Child Marriage
Drawing on the legislative framework and the community focus of BBBP, the Ministry of Women and Child Development (MWCD) launched the national BVMB campaign on 27 November 2024 with the objective of making India child-marriage-free.
It brought together Government institutions, State and Union Territory administrations, local bodies, educational institutions, frontline workers, civil society organizations, faith leaders, youth and citizens around a common national commitment. The campaign seeks to strengthen community-level prevention, improve public access to CMPOs, increase reporting of child marriage, and support girls at risk.
The campaign aims to reduce the prevalence of child marriage and to make India child-marriage-free by 2030, in line with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Target 5.3. MWCD has committed to fully funding the campaign, giving priority to 257 high-burden districts
identified through NFHS-5 data, where the prevalence of child marriage is at or above the national average.
BVMB Portal: Connecting Citizens with Action
The BVMB Portal (
https://stopchildmarriage.wcd.gov.in
) has been developed as the digital backbone of the campaign, providing a centralised platform for the effective implementation, monitoring and outreach of BVMB.
The portal makes details of Child Marriage Prohibition Officers (CMPOs) accessible to the public. It facilitates the reporting of child marriage incidents. States, Union Territories and field functionaries can also record awareness activities and community mobilisation efforts.
The portal also provides a platform for citizens, institutions and public representatives to take the BVMB pledge, the pledge initiative also being facilitated through MyGov. Thus, the portal serves as both a citizen-facing platform for information and reporting and a monitoring mechanism to track the campaign’s progress and implementation across the country.
100-Day Special Awareness Campaign
To intensify national effort at the end of the campaign’s first year, MWCD launched a 100-Day Intensive Awareness Campaign on 4 December 2025 at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi, accompanied by a synchronised national pledge-taking ceremony.
Implemented from 27 November 2025 to 8 March 2026 across all States and Union Territories, it moved in three spells from general awareness to targeted institutional engagement and, finally, to community-level commitment.
Spell and period
Focus group
Key activities
Spell I
27 November to 31 December 2025
Schools, colleges and universities
Awareness and sensitisation sessions, debates, essay competitions, interactive activities and pledge ceremonies
Spell II
1 to 31 January 2026
Religious institutions, faith leaders, community influencers and marriage-related service providers
Engagement with temples, mosques and other places of worship; outreach to caterers, tent houses, DJs and other service providers; display of Information, Education and Communication (IEC) material
Spell III
1 February to 8 March 2026
Gram Panchayats and Municipal Wards
Community mobilisation and facilitation of resolutions declaring Panchayat/Ward jurisdictions child-marriage-free
The campaign was implemented through coordinated efforts of the Central Ministries and Departments, State and Union Territory Governments, district administrations and various institutional and community-level stakeholders. The emphasis was on strengthening the role of CMPOs, mobilising local institutions and ensuring active community participation in preventing child marriages.
States and Union Territories were encouraged to undertake awareness and outreach activities, involve Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies, and strengthen monitoring at the district and grassroots levels.
Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat: Key Achievements
The BVMB Campaign has contributed to strengthening the national effort to eliminate child marriage through sustained awareness generation, institutional mobilisation, community participation and preventive action. The key achievements of the campaign are as follows:
1. Extensive Awareness and Community Outreach
6.85 lakh
awareness programmes conducted across the country.
12.47 crore
participants reached through awareness and mobilisation activities.
The 100-Day Awareness Campaign provided a structured framework for engagement with educational institutions, students, religious leaders, marriage-related service providers, Panchayati Raj Institutions, Urban Local Bodies and local communities.
2. Strengthening of the Institutional Framework
71,882 Child Marriage Prohibition Officers (CMPOs)
reflected on the BVMB Portal.
59,686 CMPOs
designated at the Gram Panchayat level, strengthening the reach of the prevention mechanism at the grassroots.
The portal provides a centralised platform for accessing CMPO details and monitoring awareness and preventive activities across States and Union Territories.
3. Increased Citizen Participation
42.01 lakh pledges
registered through the BVMB Portal and MyGov, comprising 40.96 lakh pledges through the BVMB Portal and 1.05 lakh pledges through MyGov.
The pledge initiative has provided citizens, institutions and public representatives an opportunity to affirm their commitment towards a child-marriage-free India.
4. Reporting and Preventive Action
4,536 child marriage incidents
recorded on the BVMB Portal.
Focused interventions during high-risk periods, including Akshaya Tritiya, have involved district administrations, CMPOs, law enforcement agencies and community stakeholders in efforts to prevent child marriages through timely intervention and coordinated action.
Convergence with Central Ministries and Departments, State and Union Territory Governments, district administrations and grassroots institutions has strengthened the whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach towards eliminating child marriage.
The portal supports mapping and public access to CMPO details, incident reporting, recording of awareness activities, monitoring of local mobilisation and online pledge-taking. Together, these functions promote transparency, timely reporting, evidence-based monitoring and follow-up.
Progress Across States and Union Territories
The national prevalence declined from 23.3 per cent in NFHS-5 (2019-21) to 20.1 per cent in NFHS-6 (2023-24). Most States and Union Territories show a decline since NFHS-5. Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu registered the largest reduction of 10.1 percentage points, followed by Andaman and Nicobar Islands (7.4 percentage points), Assam (6.5 percentage points), Bihar (6.2 percentage points) and Tripura (6.1 percentage points).  28 States and Union Territories are doing better than the national average, including Karnataka,
Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Mizoram and Keralam.
Two Years of Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat
The National Observance on 27 November 2026 marks two years of the BVMB campaign. Against this backdrop of stronger legal machinery, wider community participation and growing data, it provides an occasion to take stock of progress, recognise the contribution of CMPOs and grassroots stakeholders, share replicable practices from States and Union Territories, and renew the national commitment to prevention.
The continuing focus is on strengthening dedicated CMPO arrangements, improving the quality and completeness of portal data, expanding awareness and pledge mobilisation, and ensuring timely reporting and preventive intervention. It also includes deepening the participation of Panchayats, urban local bodies, educational institutions, families, faith leaders, youth and civil society.
The NFHS figures show that prevalence is falling but unevenly across States, which is why this effort must be sustained. It remains aligned with the national objective of a child-marriage-free India by 2030 and SDG Target 5.3.

title: Cheaper Cancer Medicines: What the New Margin Cap Means for Patients
subtitle: Trade margins on 137 anti-cancer medicines capped at 30% of the maximum retail price
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 NOV 2026 2:03PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Affordable, quality cancer care for every family is a priority for the Government of India. On October 17, 2026, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) capped the trade margin on 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines, including patented ones, at 30% of the maximum retail price (MRP). The revised prices take effect on November 9, 2026. By November 4, 2026, 70 companies had reported revised MRPs for 120 drugs, with the highest reduction at 96.45% and estimated savings of Rs. 3,357.49 crore. MRP reductions average 20% to 70%.
Cancer Medicine Prices Reduced by 20% to 70% on Average
The Government has capped excessive markups along the pharmaceutical supply chain, in retail and hospital pharmacies across the country, to make cancer treatment in India more affordable.
Companies have reported an average of
20% to 70%
in MRP reductions. The highest reduction reported was
96.45%
(as on November 4, 2026).
Due to these MRP reductions, the estimated savings stand at
Rs. 3,357.49 crore
(as on November 4, 2026). The estimate represents the difference between the original and revised prices, applied to the volume sold from April 2025 to March 2026.
The cap responds to concerns raised by State authorities, patients and civil society about
the gap between the procurement price
and the
Maximum Retail Price
(MRP) of anti-cancer medicines.
Consumers can verify prices using both the
NPPA website
and the official
Pharma Sahi Daam
mobile app.
The new prices are worked out from the distributor price of March 2026.
What Is a Trade Margin?
Trade margin
is the difference between the price a manufacturer charges a stockist/distributor and the highest price (MRP) a patient pays for a medicine excluding Goods and Services Tax (GST). When this trade margin is very high, large profits are added along the supply chain. This
heavily inflates the final cost for patients
, making already expensive cancer drugs far more costly than the price at which the manufacturer sells them.
The Order sets the new maximum retail price of each medicine from its average distributor price of March 2026. The trade margin within that price can be no more than 30%, and GST is added on top.
How Medicine Prices Are Regulated
To make essential life-saving drugs more affordable for patients, the Government regulates medicine prices under the
Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013
.
This is under the
mandate of the Essential Commodities Act
that seeks to regulate medicine prices, prevent profiteering and ensure essential treatments remain affordable.
DPCO, 2013 places medicines in two groups:
Scheduled medicines:
These are the medicines included in the First Schedule of the DPCO, 2013, which is the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), 2022. The Government fixes a ceiling price for each of them. The NLEM 2022 lists
388 medicines, of which 63 are anti-cancer medicines
.
Non-scheduled medicines:
These are the medicines not included in the First Schedule of the DPCO, 2013. Unlike scheduled medicines, which have a fixed ceiling price, these are regulated through price monitoring: under Paragraph 20 of the DPCO, 2013, a manufacturer may raise the MRP by no more than 10% in twelve months, and where the increase goes beyond 10%, the price must come back down to the 10% level for the next twelve months.
To address high prices beyond these scheduled essential drugs, the Government piloted a Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) intervention in 2019 covering
42 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs
, which successfully drove down patient costs.
Building on this, and on market data showing high mark-ups and gaps between retail and hospital prices, the Government invoked its
extraordinary public-interest powers
under Paragraph 19 of DPCO, 2013. On the recommendation of an Expert Committee constituted under the Directorate General of Health Services, the Authority brought
137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs
(including patented ones) under trade margin rationalisation by its Order of October 17, 2026.
What Is the National List of Essential Medicines?
The
National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)
is an official list of necessary, high-priority medicines for India. Its latest revision, NLEM 2022, was released by Union Health Minister Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya on
September 13, 2022
, under the Government’s vision of
“Sabko Dawai, Sasti Dawai”
(Medicine for everyone, affordable medicine).
History:
First created in 1996, then updated in 2003, 2011, 2015, and 2022.
Who Made It:
An expert panel called the Standing National Committee on Medicines (SNCM), after talking with doctors, scientists, industry experts, and checking WHO standards.
Why the List Matters
Lower Costs:
Helps lower out-of-pocket medical expenses for families.
Good Healthcare:
Ensures medicines are safe, effective, and good quality.
Better Planning:
Guides government buying, hospital budgets, health insurance, and training for medical students.
The Legal Power Behind the Order: Paragraph 19 of the DPCO, 2013
Special Powers for the Government:
In extraordinary circumstances, the Government can act in the public interest beyond the standard rules.
Setting or Changing Prices:
The Government has the power to set a maximum (ceiling) price or retail price for any drug for as long as it thinks is necessary.
Changing a Price Already Fixed:
If a price has already been set, the Government can raise or lower it directly, without waiting for the usual yearly revision linked to the wholesale price index.
How the New Order Limits Trade Margins on Cancer Medicines
Trade Margin Capped at 30% of the Maximum Retail Price:
The trade margin (the markup added between what the manufacturer charges the distributor and what the patient pays) cannot be more than
30%
.
Applies to All Versions:
This rule applies to all the anti-cancer drugs listed below, whatever their dose or form (pills, injections and the like) and whether they are sold alone or in combination.
Based on March 2026 Prices:
The starting price for this calculation must be the distributor price (Price to Stockist/Distributor) as of
March 2026
.

What Changes for Patients and Companies
Manufacturers must recalculate their maximum retail prices using their average distributor prices from March 2026. Free medicines given under patient assistance programmes and direct government sales do not count in this calculation.
The new lower prices will go into effect on
November 9, 2026
. Medicines that are already cheaper than the new price limit cannot be made more expensive.
Companies must inform NPPA of their revised prices. They must also publish the price cuts in newspapers, post them on their websites, and share them with all retailers and hospitals.
NPPA has put up the revised prices of these medicines on its website, and the list is updated as and when companies submit their revised prices.
By November 4, 2026, 70 companies had reported revised MRPs, covering 1,136 stock keeping units (SKUs) of 120 drugs.
Companies are not allowed to cut medicine production without permission, and they must give 6 months’ notice before stopping a medicine completely.
Hospitals and chemists must clearly display the new prices. Any company that does not lower its prices has to deposit the overcharged amount with interest.
Wider Government Support for Cancer Care
The Government runs various health programmes to provide affordable cancer care treatment, screenings and medicines for the public.
AB-PMJAY: Cashless Hospital Care, Including Cancer Treatment
The Government of India, through the Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) provides
Rs. 5 lakh per family per year
to families from the poorest 40% of society and to all senior citizens aged 70 and above.
The scheme has
authorised 12.69 crore hospital admissions worth Rs. 1.92 lakh crore
(as on June 30, 2026).
The scheme covers
cashless treatment for 1,961 procedures across 27 medical specialties, including Medical Oncology, Surgical Oncology and Radiation Oncology
, through empanelled public and private hospitals.
Under the scheme,
19.5 lakh admissions for medical oncology, worth about Rs. 2,926 crore, have been authorised
(as on November 4, 2026).
NP-NCD: Cancer Care from Screening to Treatment
The Government, through its National Programme for the Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD), which is also part of the National Health Mission, strengthens infrastructure, human resource development, screening, early diagnosis, referral, treatment and health promotion for non-communicable diseases, including cancer.
Under the NP-NCD:
770 District NCD clinics and 6,410 NCD clinics at Community Health Centres and 524 Day Care Cancer Centres
have been set up for cancer patients.
To strengthen cancer treatment infrastructure, the Government is supporting the establishment of State Cancer Institutes (SCIs), Tertiary Care Cancer Centres (TCCCs) under
the Strengthening of Tertiary Care Cancer Facilities Scheme
and DCCCs under NP-NCD to improve equitable access to quality cancer care across the country.
19 State Cancer Institutes (SCIs) and 20 Tertiary Care Cancer Centres
(TCCCs)
have been approved across the country to strengthen tertiary cancer care.
Further, Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) has established six hospitals at Varanasi, Visakhapatnam, New Chandigarh, Guwahati, Sangrur and Muzaffarpur to provide cancer care.
Cancer treatment services, including diagnostic, medical and surgical facilities, have also been extended to all 22 new AIIMS.
In addition, the National Cancer Institute (NCI), Jhajjar and the second campus of Chittaranjan National Cancer Institute (CNCI), Kolkata provide advanced diagnostic and treatment facilities.
The programme also supports population-based screening, awareness generation on risk factors, and strengthening of cancer surveillance through the National Cancer Registry Programme (NCRP) of the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR).
Screening for Common Cancers at Primary Healthcare Centres
The
Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
, which are primary health care centres across the country, also provide cancer screening in their communities.
Over
1.86 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs) are functional across the country (as on August 12, 2026).
They screen people over 30 years of age for common cancers (oral, breast and cervical), among other primary healthcare services.
Prevention, control and screening services are provided through trained frontline workers such as Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) and Auxiliary Nurse Midwives (ANMs).
Screenings carried out as on July 2026:
Oral cancer: 36.11 crore
Breast cancer: 16.94 crore
Cervical cancer: 9.31 crore
Free HPV Vaccination to Prevent Cervical Cancer
The
Nationwide Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccination Campaign
was launched on February 28, 2026 for approximately 1.2 crore eligible beneficiary girls aged 14 years across all 36 States and Union Territories.
India has administered more than
80 lakh doses of HPV vaccine free of cost
under the Campaign since its launch in February 2026 (as on September 11, 2026).
Low-Cost Medicine Outlets: Jan Aushadhi and AMRIT
The Government also runs various schemes to make essential drugs, including cancer drugs, more affordable for the common public.
They
improve access to affordable cancer medicines, stents, and implants
, reducing out-of-pocket expenses and supporting long-term treatment adherence.
Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP)
The PMBJP covers 2,110 medicines and 315 surgicals, medical consumables and devices,
covering all major therapeutic groups including cancer
.
There are
20,149 Jan Aushadhi Kendras across the country
(as on June 30, 2026).
In the five financial years from 2021-22 to 2025-26, PMBJP made sales of
Rs. 7,873.85 crore through Jan Aushadhi Kendras
across the country, which led to
savings of about Rs. 37,200 crore to the citizens
(as on March 31, 2026)
.
Affordable Medicines and Reliable Implants for Treatment Pharmacies
AMRIT (Affordable Medicines and Reliable Implants for Treatment) aims to make
medicines for cancer, cardiac diseases and other serious illnesses available at affordable prices
.
The initiative offers more than
6,500 medicines, implants, surgical products and other healthcare items at discounts of up to an average of 50%
on the Maximum Retail Price (MRP).
285 AMRIT outlets are operational
across 24 States and four Union Territories.
Since its inception, AMRIT has served
more than 8.13 crore patients
.
Medicines and healthcare products worth approximately Rs. 22,323 crore at MRP have been distributed through the network,
resulting in savings of around Rs. 10,969 crore for patients
and helping reduce their out-of-pocket healthcare expenditure (as on September 24, 2026).
Teleconsultations for Cancer Care
Teleconsultation services are provided through the
eSanjeevani platform
to improve access to specialist care, particularly in remote and underserved areas. This includes oncology care.
Over 50 crore patients have used this service
for all kinds of care, including cancer care (as on October 21, 2026).
Making Cancer Treatments Affordable and Accessible
The trade margin cap adds to the support the Government already gives at every stage of cancer care: screening at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, free HPV vaccination for girls, cashless hospital treatment under AB-PMJAY, and lower-cost medicines at Jan Aushadhi Kendras and AMRIT pharmacies. Together, these measures bring quality cancer care within reach of more families, closer to where they live.

title: Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser and DPIIT Launches API Integration between Startup India and I-STEM Portals to Strengthen Access to National Research Infrastructure
ministry: Office of Principal Scientific Advisor to GoI
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 NOV 2026 6:39PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, in collaboration with the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry, launched the API integration of DPIIT’s Startup India Portal with the Indian Science, Technology and Engineering Facilities Map (I-STEM) Portal on 6 November 2026, under the chairmanship of Prof. Ajay Kumar Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser (PSA). The initiative seeks to strengthen linkages between the startup ecosystem and the country’s research infrastructure by enabling DPIIT-recognised startups to discover and access existing scientific and testing facilities.
The launch was attended by Dr. (Mrs.) Parvinder Maini, Scientific Secretary, Office of the PSA; and Shri Ateesh Kumar Singh, Additional Secretary, DPIIT. Dr. Vishal Choudhary, Scientist-F; Dr. Santhosh Nair, Scientist-D; Dr. Shefali Uttam, Technical Staff, Office of the PSA; and members of the DPIIT and I-STEM teams were also present. Dr. Vishal Choudhary gave a brief presentation about the current status and impact of I-STEM.
Speaking on the occasion, Prof. Sood highlighted that the integration represents an institutional convergence beyond a digital interface, connecting startup requirements with the scientific infrastructure and technical capabilities available across the country. He emphasised its potential to lower R&D costs, avoid duplication of capital-intensive facilities and enhance the utilisation of publicly funded infrastructure. He also underscored the importance of stronger industry–academia linkages and access to specialised facilities for deep-tech startups across technology development, prototyping, testing and validation.
Dr. Maini highlighted I-STEM’s role in promoting the sharing and optimal utilisation of scientific infrastructure across academic and research institutions. She noted that the integration would simplify the discovery of relevant facilities for DPIIT-recognised startups, helping address infrastructure-related barriers to technology development and innovation.
Shri Ateesh Kumar Singh highlighted the role of the integration in strengthening DPIIT’s efforts to build an enabling environment for startups, particularly in the deep-tech sector. He noted that the integration would provide DPIIT-recognised startups with improved visibility of specialised research, testing and prototyping facilities, enabling them to identify suitable infrastructure, reduce the need for independent capital investment in expensive equipment, and access institutional capabilities to support product development, testing and technology validation.
The integration will facilitate seamless, API-enabled interoperability between the Startup India Portal and I-STEM, with the proposed incorporation of Single Sign-On (SSO) functionality in subsequent phases, enabling DPIIT-recognised startups to directly access and leverage I-STEM's scientific infrastructure and research facilities through the Startup India Portal. Automated verification of DPIIT recognition status and seamless linking will streamline onboarding and facilitate the discovery of scientific equipment and research facilities. While the integration simplifies the process of identifying and requesting access to infrastructure, individual requests will continue to be evaluated and approved by the respective host institutions based on technical suitability, availability, applicable charges, safety requirements and institutional permissions. As of 6 November 2026, I-STEM listed 31,540 equipment items across 4,044 registered institutions, providing a substantial national resource base for researchers and innovators.
The initiative brings together the complementary institutional strengths of DPIIT and the Office of the PSA to build a more connected and resource-efficient innovation ecosystem. Wider onboarding of research facilities, regular updation of infrastructure information and sustained engagement with startups and host institutions will be essential to maximise its reach and facilitate the translation of scientific capabilities into technology-based solutions.

1,26,052 Sq. Ft. of Office Space Freed Through Campaign Activities

3,184 Outdoor Cleanliness Campaigns Conducted

 Significant Progress in File Review, Record Weeding and Scrap Disposal
ministry: Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers :Department of Fertilizers
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 NOV 2026 6:48PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Fertilizers (DoF) and its Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) successfully implemented Special Campaign 6 from 2 October to 31 October 2026. The campaign aimed to institutionalize Swachhata, reduce pendency and enhance efficiency in government offices, in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG).
As part of #SpecialCampaign6, The Fertilisers And Chemicals Travancore Limited organized a cleanliness drive at the #PMKSK, Udupi, Karnataka, in accordance with the Department of Fertilizers' directives. Before and After photographs highlight the remarkable improvement. https://t.co/wHogIvfHrM
— Department of Fertilizers (@BharatUrvarak)
October 29, 2026
As of 31 October 2026, the Department and its PSUs have made significant progress in reviewing physical files and e-files, weeding out old records, disposing of scrap materials and improving cleanliness in office premises. The campaign also focused on the disposal of public grievances, appeals and other pending matters.
Key Achievements as of 31 October 2026
The Department and its PSUs recorded the following achievements under Special Campaign 6 :
Review of Physical Files: 14,190 physical files reviewed against 81,00 files identified for review.
E-File Management: 7,257 e-files reviewed against a target of 637, out of which 6,783 successfully closed.
Weeding Out of Records: 2,705 physical files weeded out against 5,516 files identified for weeding.
Cleanliness Drives: 3,184 outdoor cleanliness campaigns conducted by the Department and its PSUs, including cleanliness activities at PMKSKs.
Scrap Disposal: Revenue of ₹87,54,854 generated through the disposal of office scrap.
Space Freed: 1,26,052 square feet of space freed, enabling better utilization of office premises.
Public Grievance Appeals: All public grievance and appeals reported in the campaign data have been disposed of.
Social Media Outreach
As part of Special Campaign 6, the Department published more than 100 social media posts to raise awareness about cleanliness and efficient office management. These posts were disseminated through social media platforms such as  X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp Channel and the PIB X handle.

October 28, 2026
The posts highlighted cleanliness drives, records management, proper disposal of e-waste and scrap, and other campaign-related activities, thereby promoting awareness about Swachhata and efficient governance.
Special Campaign 6 Concludes
Special Campaign 6 concluded on 31 October 2026. The Department of Fertilizers and its PSUs remain committed to sustaining cleanliness, reducing pendency, improving workplace efficiency and ensuring the proper disposal of obsolete records, e-waste and scrap materials.
The campaign reflects the Government of India’s commitment to promoting cleanliness, improving efficiency and creating cleaner and more organized workplaces.
